title: What is Medicaid?
summary: Explains Medicaid as a federal and state program, who it serves, plan types, enrollment statistics, mandatory and optional benefits, home and community-based services, and how to apply.

atoms.title: Medicaid is a federal and state program
atoms.question: What is Medicaid?
atoms.text: Medicaid is a federal and state program that provides health care coverage to people who qualify. Each state runs its own Medicaid program, but the federal government has rules that all states must follow. The federal government also provides at least half of the funding for their Medicaid requirements. Coverage is based on income and the value of what you own.

Who pays for Medicaid?
Is Medicaid run by the federal government or the state?

atoms.title: States can offer more than federal minimums
atoms.question: Can states offer more than the federal government requires under Medicaid?
atoms.text: Based on federal regulations, states create and run their own Medicaid program to best serve residents who qualify. States may choose to provide more services than the federal government requires, and they may also choose to provide coverage to larger groups of people. Each state decides the full range of benefits that it covers under Medicaid.

Can my state add extra Medicaid benefits?

atoms.title: Medicaid began with the Social Security Act of 1965
atoms.question: When did Medicaid start?
atoms.text: Medicaid began as part of the Social Security Act of 1965. The original law gave states the option of receiving federal funding to help provide health care coverage to children whose families have a low income, their caregiver relatives, people who are blind and people who are disabled. Over time, the federal government has strengthened the rules and requirements for state Medicaid programs.
questions: When was Medicaid created?
What was the original purpose of Medicaid?

atoms.title: Who Medicaid serves
atoms.question: Who does Medicaid serve?
atoms.text: Medicaid programs serve specific groups of people, including pregnant women with low income, children of low-income families, children in foster care, people with disabilities, seniors with low income, and parents or caregivers with low income. States can also choose to expand eligibility to other groups, such as people with low income who may or may not have children.

atoms.title: Medicaid, D-SNP and CHIP plan types
atoms.question: What types of Medicaid-related plans are available?
atoms.text: Depending on the state, there may be several types of low-cost or no-cost plans. Medicaid is managed by each state and may have its own state name. Dual Eligible Special Needs plans (D-SNP) cover people who qualify for both Medicare and Medicaid, and most give more benefits than Original Medicare. The Children's Health Insurance Program (CHIP) offers low-cost or no-cost coverage for infants, children and teens.

atoms.title: Medicaid and CHIP enrollment numbers
atoms.question: How many people are enrolled in Medicaid and CHIP?
atoms.text: According to the Medicaid.gov August 2020 Enrollment Report, 76.4 million individuals were enrolled in Medicaid and CHIP. Of those, 69.7 million individuals were enrolled in Medicaid and 6.6 million individuals were enrolled in CHIP.

How many children are enrolled in CHIP?

atoms.title: Mandatory Medicaid benefits
atoms.question: What are the mandatory Medicaid benefits?
atoms.text: Federal law requires states to provide certain benefits, called mandatory benefits. They include inpatient and outpatient hospital services, early and periodic screening, diagnostic and treatment services (EPSDT), nursing facility services, home health services, physician services, rural health clinic and federally qualified health center services, laboratory and X-ray services, family planning, nurse midwife services, transportation to medical care and tobacco cessation counseling for pregnant women.
questions: What does Medicaid have to cover?
Is transportation to medical care a required Medicaid benefit?

atoms.title: Optional Medicaid benefits
atoms.question: What are optional Medicaid benefits?
atoms.text: States may choose to offer other benefits, called optional benefits. These include prescription drugs, clinic services, physical and occupational therapy, speech and hearing services, podiatry, optometry, dental services, dentures, prosthetics, eyeglasses, chiropractic services, private duty nursing, personal care, hospice, case management, self-directed personal assistance services and health homes for enrollees with chronic conditions.
questions: Does Medicaid cover dental or eyeglasses?
Which Medicaid benefits are optional?

atoms.title: All states include some prescription drug coverage
atoms.question: Does Medicaid cover prescription drugs?
atoms.text: Prescription drug coverage is an optional benefit under federal Medicaid law. But, as of 2020, all states include some form of prescription drug coverage under their Medicaid program. In general, most enrollees within a state Medicaid program will get prescription drug coverage.
questions: Are prescriptions covered by Medicaid?
Do all states cover drugs under Medicaid?

atoms.title: Medicaid home and community-based services
atoms.question: What home and community-based services (HCBS) does Medicaid cover?
atoms.text: Medicaid programs may cover Home- and Community-Based Services (HCBS) to help people stay living at home and active in their community. Examples include personal care like showering, transportation, skilled nursing care, occupational, speech and physical therapy, diet and nutrition management, home-delivered meals and home chores and housekeeping. The level of support is typically based on the individual's needs.

atoms.title: How to apply for Medicaid
atoms.question: How do I apply for Medicaid?
atoms.text: Because each state manages its own Medicaid program, eligibility varies from one state to another. 1) If you have questions about qualifying, contact your state Medicaid agency. 2) Or apply online at the website for your state Medicaid agency to see if you qualify. 3) Answer a few quick questions on the plan-eligibility tool to see what type of plan may be a good fit. Benefits change depending on where you live.
